An ad insix steps.

A 36-second reel about how we build a product ad that stops the scroll: cut it out, build it a world, one font, motion on every word, a sound for everything you see, and the cover. Everything on screen is drawn in code on an HTML canvas, in paper collage, timed to the voice word by word. Below: the six steps with a prompt for each, and how the reel itself was made.

01 · The idea

Six steps, one ad.

A product ad that stops the scroll isn't one big idea; it's six small decisions done well, in order. The reel shows them on one invented product, a perfume called BRISA: from a photo in a cluttered magazine page to a finished ad with its own world, type, motion, sound and cover.

It opens on a board with the six steps and a feed that freezes on the ad, pulls out the step everyone forgets (the cover), walks through the six steps one block each, and closes with the board fully checked and a wall of other ads made the same way.

02 · The six steps

All six, ready to copy.

This is what you asked for in the comments. One prompt per step, in order. Run them in Claude Code inside a folder with your product photo and your voiceover; check a still at every step before moving on.

step 1 · cut it out
Step 1 · Cut it out.
Here is my product photo: [file]. Cut the product out cleanly, with no leftover background and no halo.
Save it as a PNG with transparency, trimmed to the product. Then show it to me on a dark and a light
background at 200% so I can check the edges, and tell me where the cut is soft.
step 2 · build it a world
Step 2 · Build it a world.
Build a world for this product, drawn in code (HTML canvas), in a 9:16 frame. My brand colours: [#hex, #hex, #hex].
The idea of the product: [e.g. "it smells like the sea"]. Make the world say that idea with 3-4 layers
(background colours, a texture, a light source, one element of the idea), and put the product in it with a real shadow.
Show me one still before animating anything.

Why a world and not a background: a flat colour behind a product says nothing. Three or four layers that tell the product's one idea (here: the sea, because brisa means breeze) make the ad readable without words.

step 3 · one font, one word
Step 3 · One font, one word.
Give me three font options for the headline (one serif, one grotesk, one display), each set with my line:
"[your headline]". Pick one with me. Then set the headline so ONE word carries it (bigger, italic or in the accent
colour) and the rest stays small. No more than one font plus the brand's body font.
step 4 · make it move
Step 4 · Make it move.
Here is the voiceover: [file]. Transcribe it with a time for every word. Then animate the ad so every motion lands on a
word: the product enters on its name, the headline word slams on that word, the world moves on the verbs.
Something moves at least every second. Render a stills sheet (one frame every 1.5 s) before the video.

The rule that changes everything: every motion lands on a word of the voice. If it moves on the beat of a word, the viewer feels it was edited; if it moves on its own clock, it feels like a template.

step 5 · add sound
Step 5 · Add sound.
List every visible event of the video with its time (things that enter, hit, pour, open, tap). Give each one a short
sound that matches its material (glass, paper, water, a cap), no more than one sound every 1.2 s, nothing as filler.
Mix the voice on top, sounds about 18 dB under it, final loudness -14 LUFS, peak -1.5 dB.
step 6 · the cover
Step 6 · The cover.
Make the cover for this ad: 1080x1920, but everything important between y 300 and y 1480 (the feed crops it to 4:5).
Use the strongest frame of the video, the product big, the headline short and readable on a phone, the brand colours
at full strength. Show it next to 8 grey squares like a profile grid so I can check that it stands out.
Check 01

One still per step.

Look at a frame before going on. Fixing a cut-out after the motion is done costs ten times more.

Check 02

Phone size.

Look at every still at phone size. If the headline doesn't read there, it doesn't read.

Check 03

The grid.

Put the cover next to grey squares. If it doesn't jump out of the grid, nobody taps it.

03 · References

A tutorial's format, our own look.

The format was studied from a step-by-step tutorial reel, for its structure only: a step badge with progress dots and a board of numbered steps. Its content, words and presenter were not used. The look is new for the Lab: paper collage in risograph colours.

An invented product

BRISA, an eau de parfum in a faceted glass bottle with a gold cap, drawn entirely in code, first as a magazine photo and then as a clean cut-out.

Paper collage

Torn edges with a white fibre core, masking tape, halftone dots, misregistered print and a torn-paper wipe between blocks.

A colour per block

Cream, ink, pink, blue, yellow at full strength, light and dark alternating so every step starts on a new paper.

#F4EDE1 cream#141210 ink#FF4F8B pink#2B4BFF blue#FFD23F yellow
A presenter inside the scene

Catalina, from her real images and clips only, stands behind real objects of each block (the magazine page, the paper waves, the timeline, the board) and her faces become part of the scene: a forgotten note, reactions to the fonts, the profile picture, the commenters.

04 · Claude session

One kit, then two builders.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 36-second vertical edu reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. Topic: how we build a product ad that stops the scroll, in six steps Claude does with us.

1. Script (use it word for word): "A product ad that stops the scroll takes six steps, and Claude does every one of them with us. The last step is the one everyone forgets. First, cut out the product, clean, no leftover background. Then build it a world: colors, paper, light, all made in code. Pick one font, and let one word carry the line. Now make it move, every motion landing on a word. Give it a sound for everything you see. And last, the cover, because that's what makes people tap. That's how every ad on this page gets made. Comment AD and we'll send you all six steps."

2. Voice. ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", natural speed (1.0), every word's start and end saved; every cue reads a word time.

3. Product. Invent one: BRISA, an eau de parfum in a faceted glass bottle with a gold cap, drawn in code. Show it first inside a cluttered magazine photo, then cut out.

4. Look. Paper collage, risograph: torn edges, masking tape, halftone dots, misregistered print, Anton for the step titles with one word in the accent. One full-strength paper colour per block (cream, ink, pink, blue, yellow), light and dark alternating. A step badge with six progress dots, and a 6-step board that opens and closes the reel.

5. Rhythm. An event on every stressed word, nothing still for more than 1.2 s, the stage full within 2-3 s of every block. Data notes with this reel's real numbers (hex colours, frames, sounds, cover size), stamps, hand-drawn arrows and counters.

6. Presenter. Our presenter appears in every block, big and always behind a real object of the scene (the magazine page, the paper waves, the timeline strip, the film strip, the board), or as faces inside the scene (a note, an avatar, the commenters). Nothing important below y 1480.

7. Process. Build a shared kit, show me the stills, then build the blocks in parallel. Run the motion and originality checks before the final render.

What came back: a block-by-block storyboard, the narration with 104 time-stamped words, a shared kit (torn paper, tape, the step badge, the 6-step board, the BRISA bottle, data notes and stamps) and two builders making five blocks each at the same time from the same kit and word clock.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds from frame 0, with the presenter composited and the safe-zone guide in red. Check that every block is full at its cut, the presenter is hidden at the waist by a real object, and the text reads on a phone. Fix everything in one pass.

What came back: 36.5 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, 14 Mbps, the voice plus 74 sound effects on real events, mixed at −14 LUFS. The skill's motion check: 8.5 motion, 1.5 big moments per second, 2% still.

06 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Pull out the forgotten step

The cover is announced in the second line, before the steps start, so the viewer waits for it until the end.

02

Real numbers, not decoration

Every note on screen is true for this reel: the hex colours, 30 fps, the frame count, 74 sounds, the 1080×1350 cover.

03

Behind, never floating

A half-body presenter floating on paper looks like a sticker. Hiding her waist behind a real object of the scene makes her part of it.

04

Every cue is a word

The scissors snip on "cut", the sun rises on "light", the stamp lands on "word", the cover pops on "tap".
